The United States has evidence that some Chinese state-owned companies
might provide non-lethal assistance to Russia for its invasion of Ukraine.

even though Washington wants other countries
to distance themselves from Russia.
Data show that in 2022,
China's imports from Russia increased by nearly 50%,
while exports rose 13%.
A Chinese engineer has been sentenced to eight years in prison
for being a part of Beijing's efforts
to extract advanced aerospace and satellite technologies
developed by U.S. entities.

January 25th,

Shu Yanjun,

Shu was sentenced to 20 years behind bars last year
after being found guilty of trade secret theft
targeting GE Aviation and other aviation firms.
The DOJ said Chinese engineer Ji was part of Beijing's efforts
to obtain cutting-edge aeronautical and satellite technology
being developed by companies within the U.S.
Ji arrived in the U.S. via a student visa in 2013.
One year after his graduation in 2016,
he enlisted in the U.S. Army Reserves
under a program that allows foreigners to be recruited,
providing their abilities are deemed vital to the national interest,
shortly called the MAVNI program.
However, the Chinese national falsely claimed that he had no interaction
with a foreign government in the seven years leading to his application.
In subsequent interviews with a U.S. Army officer,
he also didn't reveal his connection to Chinese intelligence agents.
Ji met an undercover agent disguised as a minister of state security multiple times.
During this,
he told the person that he could take photos of Roosevelt-class aircraft carriers.
He also divulged that he could access all databases from the CIA,
FBI or NASA once he obtained his U.S. citizenship and security clearance through the MAVNI program.
Last September,
Washington convicted Ji of acting as an agent for a foreign government illegally,
a charge used in espionage cases.
He was also found guilty of making false statements to the U.S. Army.
The Chinese regime can spy on millions of people in the U.K.
by weaponizing microchips in cars, household appliances and even light bulbs.
According to a report from the Washington-based consultancy
Observe, Orientate, Decide, Act ,
small modules known as cellular IoT,
Internet of Things can gather and transmit data by using the 5G network.
The Telegraph reported that this allows the Chinese regime to track any entity that uses the device,
targeting both military intelligence and industrial espionage.
The devices containing the modules include laptops, voice-controlled smart speakers,
smart watches, smart energy meters and fridges, among others.
Charles Parton, the author of the report and former diplomat, said,
We are not yet awake to this threat.
China has spotted an opportunity to dominate this market,
and if it does so, it can harvest an awful lot of data as well as making foreign countries dependent on them.
Parton warned,
It's time to wake up. Free and open countries should ban Chinese manufactured IoT modules from their supply chains as soon as possible.
According to Telegraph, three Chinese firms, China Mobile, Fibocom, and Quectel dominate the global market,
representing 54% international market share in the devices and 75% by connectivity.
Under the Chinese regime's law, all Chinese firms must hand over data to the Chinese Communist Party
if they are ordered to do so.
This means that the Chinese Communist Party can access any device with the Chinese modules.
Earlier this month, Chinese tracking devices were found in a UK government vehicle.
The report recommends a complete audit of UK government property to replace the devices.
It also suggests companies operating in sensitive fields, like defense firms, should be asked to conduct the audit.
Alicia Kearns, chairwoman of the UK's Commons Foreign Affairs Select Committee,
said that the national security concerns have been woefully inadequate when it comes to industrial strategy.

Because they are in so many of our mundane, day-to-day objects, the risk if someone was able to weaponize them is significant.
